newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed says PM must take over while Yeltsin ill.
newsitem.headline: Lebed says PM must take over while Yeltsin ill.

text.p: Security tsar Alexander Lebed, seeking to end talk of a power struggle in the Kremlin, said on Friday Boris Yeltsin should name Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to run Russia while the president is ill.
Lebed told NTV commercial television he had discussed the issue with presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais on Friday, a day after Yeltsin said he would undergo heart surgery.

"A situation has arisen where someone (Yeltsin) is temporarily unable to carry out his duties. For that period, by his order or decree, a person who would run the country and be responsible for what is going on should be clearly defined and named -- and his name is Chernomyrdin," Lebed said.
A top surgeon told Interfax news agency Yeltsin was to have a relatively routine bypass operation to relieve the ischaemia which put the 65-year-old leader in hospital twice last year.
Under the constitution, if the president is unable to carry out his duties, the prime minister stands in for him for up to three months, after which new elections must be held.
But Lebed said Yeltsin should officially name Chernomyrdin to prevent people acting in the president's name.
"There must be a juridically defined period of time when the president is dealing with his personal affairs and somebody is taking on all obligations to run the country," Lebed said.

Yeltsin's prolonged absence from the political centre stage -- he has rarely been seen in public since late June -- has sparked speculation about a power vacuum in the Kremlin and a struggle for influence between Lebed, Chubais and Chernomyrdin.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, whom Yeltsin defeated after an energy-sapping presidential election campaign, earlier on Friday called for a meeting of parliamentary faction leaders to help avert a "destabilisation" of the political situation.
"We should do all we can so that the law triumphs in this situation and not the 'viziers' who might use the president's illness, as ever, for their own self-serving ends," Zyuganov told Interfax.

The main target of the communists, who could mount another serious campaign if Yeltsin were to die or step down, appeared to be Chubais -- whose commitment to radical economic reform has made him deeply unpopular.
Chubais and Lebed also discussed the peace plan Lebed agreed last week with Chechen rebels, who on Friday celebrated the fifth anniversary of their region's declaration of independence.
Asked if he had approved the plan, which has halted months of fighting, Lebed merely said Chubais had listened attentively.

Professor Valery Sadrikov, deputy director of the Surgical Centre of the Academy of Medical Sciences, told Interfax Yeltsin would undergo "a shunt of the vessels which supply blood to the heart -- a generally routine bypass procedure in which a vein is grafted in to divert blood from clogged cardiac arteries.
The operation would be carried out at the Moscow Cardiological Centre headed by Yevgeny Chazov, Sadrikov said.
Chazov, who made his name treating Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev, said Yeltsin would make the final choice on where the operation would be.
Chazov told Interfax a council of doctors would determine whether the president was fit enough to withstand an operation.
"The question of whether the patient's health allows the operation to be carried out is decided by the council," he said.
Chazov said doctors at his unit had already conducted "coronorography" tests on the president as an out-patient.
These had shown the need for an operation on the blood vessels supplying his heart. Chazov said there was no need to replace any heart valves, as was sometimes necessary.

Millions of bypass operations have been carried out around the world since the 1960s, including in Russia, and doctors say only about two percent of patients die as a result. Within a month most can return to work and go on to live for many years.
